preamble: Glide formation turns the close front vowel [i] into the palatal approximant [j] before another vowel. Between Classical Latin and Proto-Romance, unstressed front vowels in hiatus became /j/ (fīlius > /ˈfiːljus/), and so did stressed ones in the antepenult, with the stress moving to the following vowel (fīliolus > /fiːˈljolus/). French has the same process synchronically and optionally: an underlying high vowel becomes a glide before another vowel, so that nie [ni] alternates with nier [nje] (Wiktionary also gives unglided /ni.e/), but usually not after an obstruent + liquid onset.

examples.note: The stressed i of the antepenult also became /j/, and the stress moved to the following vowel.
The stressed i of the antepenult became /j/ and the stress moved to the following vowel; the resulting /je/ later merged to /eː/ (/paˈreːteːs/).

languageExamples.context: Before a vowel, optionally (Wiktionary also gives unglided /ni.e/, /li.e/); usually not after an obstruent + liquid onset
